R03-D-01: When a job that was once filled by school leavers begins to advertise for graduates, the usual explanation is that the work has become more demanding. Machines have taken over the routine tasks, the story goes, and what remains calls for the analytical habits that only a university can supply. There is something to this. Some occupations really have changed beyond recognition, and an office clerk today handles systems that would have baffled a clerk of fifty years ago. But the explanation is offered far more often than it is checked, and when one looks at what people in many of these jobs actually do, the change in the work is often modest beside the change in the paperwork required to get it. A more economical account treats the degree less as a certificate of skill than as a ticket in a queue. When few people held degrees, an employer who asked for one was selecting a small group who were, on average, more persistent and better connected than the rest. As degrees became common, the same requirement no longer separated anyone, and employers who wanted to keep selecting raised the bar again, asking for a master's where a bachelor's had once sufficed. Each employer is behaving sensibly; it is merely using the cheapest filter available. Yet the sum of these sensible choices resembles a crowd at a parade in which everyone stands on tiptoe: no one sees better than before, and everyone is more tired. The costs of this arrangement are not evenly spread. Students from families that can afford several years of fees and forgone earnings keep pace with the rising bar; those who cannot are shut out of work they could perfectly well perform. A requirement introduced in the name of competence thus ends up rewarding the capacity to pay for time. Meanwhile the graduates themselves often discover that much of what they studied is barely used in the job, and that what the employer valued was the signal rather than the substance. None of this is an argument against education, which has goods that no labour market can measure. It is an argument against confusing two things that the word 'qualification' runs together: what a person can do, and how long a person has been able to stay in school. Some employers have begun to test applicants directly on the tasks the job involves. Where this is done, an awkward question comes into view, namely whether the degree requirement it replaces was ever a guarantee of quality or merely a habit that nobody had thought to examine.
R03-D-02: We tend to think of the weekend as a natural feature of the calendar, as if two days of rest had always followed five of work. In fact the arrangement is fairly recent, and its history suggests that free time is not simply the absence of work but something that has to be made, defended and shaped. Before the factory, many artisans worked in bursts, labouring late into the night to finish an order and then taking a day or two off whenever it suited them; in parts of England the habit of stretching Sunday's rest into Monday was common enough to be given a mock saint's name, 'Saint Monday'. Factory production could not tolerate this irregularity. Machines were expensive and had to run whenever the hands were present, and an employer could not plan production around workers who might drift in on Tuesday, so the long struggle over hours was therefore also a struggle over the shape of time. Workers wanted fewer hours; employers wanted predictable ones. The compromise that eventually emerged, first a half-day on Saturday and later the whole of it, gave each side part of what it sought. Workers won rest that was guaranteed rather than snatched, and employers won a workforce that turned up, sober, on Monday morning. It would be wrong to see the outcome merely as a defeat dressed up as a victory. For most working people, guaranteed free time was a real gain, and it was won against resistance. But the weekend also changed what free time was. Leisure that had once been taken at the worker's discretion became a fixed block, the same for everyone, and a block that was the same for everyone could be sold to. Football matches, excursion trains and seaside resorts arranged themselves around Saturday afternoon and Sunday, and leisure came increasingly to mean something one went out and paid for at a scheduled time. The lesson is not that the old irregular rhythm was better; it was often tied to poverty, to insecurity and to binges of overwork that left people exhausted. It is that arguments about working hours are never only about quantity. When people today argue over flexible schedules or a four-day week, they are reopening a question that the industrial age settled in one particular way: not merely how much time should be free, but who decides when it falls and what it is for.
R03-D-03: In the large households of the nineteenth century, the best servant was the one who was least noticed. Grand houses were built with back staircases so that maids carrying coal or slops need never meet the family on the main stairs, and bells rang in a basement corridor so that a summons could be issued without anyone having to see who answered it. In some houses servants were expected to turn aside, even to face the wall, when a member of the family passed. It is tempting to read all this as snobbery, a taste for keeping inferiors out of sight, but snobbery explains less than it seems to. The invisibility of servants was not a by-product of the genteel household; it was one of the things the household was for. What a gentleman's house displayed, above all, was ease: meals that appeared, fires that were lit, linen that was clean, all without visible effort. The ease was manufactured by a great deal of labour, and the labour had to be hidden for the ease to be believed. A servant glimpsed scrubbing a step was a reminder that comfort had a cost and a source; a servant unseen allowed the family to experience comfort as a natural condition of their kind of life. In this sense the architecture of concealment did not merely reflect a social hierarchy but helped to produce one, by allowing one class to appear exempt from necessity. Large-scale domestic service of this kind has largely disappeared, and it is easy to assume that its logic went with it. Yet much of the modern service economy seems designed to recreate the same experience by other means. Food arrives at the door from a kitchen the customer never sees, carried by a courier who is a first name on a screen. Offices are cleaned at night, after the staff have gone home. Apps promise that groceries, laundry and repairs will simply happen, and their designers speak, revealingly, of removing friction, as though the friction in question were not, very often, the encounter with another person who is doing the work. The comparison must not be pressed too far. The modern courier or cleaner is not bound to a single household, keeps hours that end, and has legal protections that a Victorian scullery maid lacked; to call such workers servants is to erase real gains. But the aspiration that the old houses expressed in brick and bells, the wish to receive service without meeting the server, has proved remarkably durable. What has changed is less the wish than the means of satisfying it, and the means are now available to far more people than ever owned a back staircase.
R03-D-04: The idea that some jobs require workers to manage their own feelings, and not merely their hands or their minds, has travelled a long way from its origins in the study of flight attendants and debt collectors. It now turns up in discussions of nursing, teaching, retail and call centres, and even of the unpaid work of keeping a family cheerful. This expansion has drawn a predictable objection: if every job involves some management of emotion, the critics say, then the concept marks out nothing in particular. A surgeon must stay calm, a lawyer must appear confident, and a builder who loses his temper with clients will not keep them; are these, too, emotional labourers? The objection is fair against the loose use of the term, but it misses what the original idea was pointing at. The distinction was never between jobs that involve feeling and jobs that do not. It was between feeling that a worker manages according to her own judgement and feeling whose display is specified, monitored and sold by someone else. The surgeon's calm serves the operation and is left to her; nobody scripts it. The call-centre agent, by contrast, may be told how often to use the customer's name, scored on the warmth of her voice, and disciplined for a sigh. The emotion is part of the product, and the employer, not the worker, sets its terms. Seen this way, the concept is narrower than its popular use suggests, but also sharper. It directs attention not to the presence of emotion at work but to its ownership, and it suggests where the cost of such work lies. Most people can smile at a stranger without harm; the difficulty arises when the smile must be produced on demand, for hours, regardless of how the worker is treated, and when failing to produce it is a disciplinary matter. One would expect work of this kind to produce a fatigue unlike ordinary tiredness, and perhaps an uncertainty about which friendly feelings are one's own. None of this implies that friendliness in service is a sham, or that customers who enjoy it are dupes. Many workers take pride in easing a stranger's day, and a scripted greeting can be delivered with real goodwill. The point is that goodwill freely given and goodwill required by contract are different things, even when they look identical from the other side of the counter, and a concept that cannot tell them apart has lost the very thing that made it worth having.
R03-D-05: For a long time the sociology of taste worked with a simple map. At the top of the social order sat a refined culture of opera, poetry and the old masters, at the bottom sat popular entertainments, and a person's place in society could be read, with fair accuracy, from the position of their preferences on this ladder. Elites, on this picture, distinguished themselves by what they refused. Liking the wrong music was not merely a private failing but a mark of origin. Surveys of cultural consumption in a number of wealthy countries have since complicated the map. The most educated and affluent groups, it turns out, are no longer best described as snobs who like only high culture. They are more often omnivores: they go to the opera and to the cinema, read literary fiction and crime novels, and are happy to discuss both a string quartet and a pop album. Some observers have greeted this as the end of cultural hierarchy, a sign that the old boundaries between high and low have dissolved and that taste has become a matter of individual preference rather than of class. That conclusion is premature. Breadth of taste is itself unevenly distributed, because it requires money, time, travel and, above all, the confidence to move between worlds without feeling out of place. The person who can talk knowledgeably about both a symphony and a street-food stall has accumulated a cultural range that is far harder to acquire than a liking for either alone. Moreover, omnivores rarely consume popular forms in the same way as their usual audiences. They tend to approach them with a knowing, curatorial attitude, prizing a song for its place in the history of a genre or enjoying a film with a touch of irony, and this manner of liking can mark distance as effectively as refusal once did. Nor is the omnivore's appetite unlimited. Research on what people say they dislike has suggested that the forms most often rejected by the highly educated tend to be those most associated with the least educated, so that the boundary has moved rather than vanished. None of this means that the loosening of old hierarchies is an illusion; it is a genuine change that the opera house must now compete for prestige with a well-chosen food truck. But distinction has not disappeared with the decline of snobbery. It has learned to express itself through openness, and openness is harder to criticise than exclusion because it looks so much like a virtue.
R03-D-06: Two accounts of the professions have long competed for our assent, and each is right about something. The first, which professionals themselves favour, holds that a profession is defined by esoteric knowledge put at the service of clients who cannot judge it. Because a patient cannot assess a diagnosis or a litigant a legal argument, the state licenses practitioners, and the licence is a guarantee of competence that protects the public from charlatans. The second account, favoured by economists of a sceptical turn, treats the same licence as a barrier to entry: by limiting the number who may practise, a profession raises its fees, and its talk of public protection is simply the language in which a cartel describes itself. What the two accounts share is more interesting than what divides them. Both look at one profession at a time, as if each stood alone facing its clients, and both assume that the work a profession does is simply given: there are diseases, so there are doctors; there are disputes, so there are lawyers. Yet the boundaries of professional work are anything but given. Whether persistent unhappiness is a medical condition, a psychological difficulty, a spiritual crisis or a social problem is not settled by the nature of unhappiness. It is settled, provisionally and repeatedly, by contests among psychiatrists, psychologists, clergy and social workers, each of whom claims that the problem properly belongs to it. Seen from this angle, a profession is less a guild guarding a fixed territory than one party in a system of rival claims, and its history is a history of conquests and retreats. Licensing remains important, but as a weapon in a jurisdictional struggle rather than as either a certificate or a mere device for fixing prices. Knowledge, too, matters in a different way. What wins a contested problem is often not superior skill in treating it but a more abstract body of theory, one that allows a profession to redefine the problem in its own terms and so to argue that its rivals were treating the symptoms rather than the thing itself. A profession whose knowledge is purely practical can be displaced by one that can explain why that practice works. This does not mean that competence is irrelevant or that the cartel theorist is merely cynical. Clients are protected by licensing, and fees are raised by it. But neither effect explains why some professions grow while others shrink, or why a body of practitioners who are perfectly good at their work can find that work quietly reassigned to others. The fate of a profession, on this view, depends less on how well it does what it does than on its ability to persuade others, including the state and the public, that the problems of the moment are its problems.
R03-D-07: The phrase 'conspicuous consumption', coined by Thorstein Veblen in the 1890s, named a habit of the wealthy of his day: the purchase of goods whose chief use was to show that one could afford them. The mansion, the carriage and the idle household were, on this account, less comforts than advertisements. The idea proved so useful that it outlived the society that prompted it, and it still shapes how we picture status spending: the logo on the handbag, the oversized car, the watch that costs more than a year's rent. The picture now misleads more than it reveals, at least at the top. As mass production and global supply chains have made once-rare goods cheap, the handbag and the car have become available, in passable imitations, to almost anyone with a credit card. Display of this kind has lost much of its power to separate, and many of the most advantaged households have turned away from it. Their spending flows instead into things that are hard to see and harder to copy: private tuition and a house in the right school catchment, retirement savings, organic groceries, exercise classes, domestic help that frees time for reading, and clothing whose quality is recognised only by those who know what to look for. The signal, where there is one, is addressed to a narrow audience of peers rather than to the street. The pattern has come to be called inconspicuous consumption. It would be easy to treat the change as an improvement in taste, a retreat from vulgar display into quieter and more sensible habits. In part it is. Much of this spending yields real benefits in health, in learning and in security, and few would wish the rich to return to buying gold-plated taps. But the shift has two consequences that the language of good taste conceals. The first is that inconspicuous goods are more effective at reproducing advantage than conspicuous ones ever were. A diamond can be sold; a childhood spent in good schools, with books at home and parents who have time, becomes part of a person and can neither be taken away nor easily acquired later. Spending of this kind does not merely display a position; it passes it on. The second consequence is moral. Conspicuous consumption invited criticism precisely because it was conspicuous. The flashy car was an obvious target for the satirist and the moralist, and its owner could be accused of vanity. Inconspicuous consumption is much harder to criticise, because it presents itself not as display but as virtue: one is not showing off, one is merely eating well, looking after one's health and investing in one's children. The vocabulary that surrounds it, of wellness, sensible choices and doing the best for one's family, offers the satirist nothing obviously vulgar to mock. Those who cannot afford to do the same are not envied so much as quietly judged, as though their diets and their children's results were failures of character rather than of income. None of this is an accusation of bad faith. It does not require us to think the affluent hypocritical, or the parent paying for tuition secretly bent on buying status; most such choices are made sincerely, for the reasons people give. The point is structural rather than personal. A society in which advantage is transmitted through the visible accumulation of objects at least makes its inequalities legible. One in which advantage flows through habits, schooling and time has made them harder to see, and inequalities that are hard to see are also harder to argue about.
R03-D-08: Few political promises are as widely shared as the promise of social mobility. Parties that agree on little else agree that a child's prospects should not be fixed by the circumstances of her birth, and the claim that mobility has stalled is one of the most damaging charges that can be laid against a government. Yet the word covers two quite different things, and much public argument about it goes astray because the two are run together. The first is absolute mobility: the share of people who end up better off than their parents, whether by income or by the kind of work they do. The second is relative mobility: the extent to which a person's position in the distribution, as opposed to their standard of living, differs from their parents' position. The two can move independently. In a period of rapid growth and expanding professional employment, most children may outearn their parents and many may enter occupations their parents never held, even if the chance of a child born near the bottom reaching the top, compared with that of a child born near the top, has not changed at all. Everyone rides the escalator up, but the order of people on it stays the same. This distinction explains a puzzle. When growth slows and the expansion of professional jobs levels off, absolute mobility falls, and people who do no better than their parents feel, reasonably enough, that something has closed. They often conclude that society has become less fair. Imagine a town where a mill employed one generation and new offices employed the next. The children did better than their parents without anyone being pushed aside, and the town experienced this as openness. When the offices stop hiring, the grandchildren find that the climb has ended. Yet on the measures that track their position against the children of the office managers, the chances may be much as they were: what has disappeared is not openness but the rising tide that once let a whole generation move up without anyone having to move down. The sense of closure is real; its diagnosis is frequently mistaken. The distinction also exposes an awkwardness that politicians prefer to leave unspoken. Absolute mobility can, in principle, be enjoyed by everyone at once. Relative mobility cannot. If positions are ranked, then for one family to climb another must fall, and a serious commitment to relative mobility is therefore a commitment to downward mobility for some children of the comfortable. It is not surprising that the comfortable resist it, often without any sense of doing so, through the ordinary devices of private tuition, a well-placed word, or the purchase of a house near the right school. Each of these looks like ordinary care for one's own children; together they amount to a defence of position. None of this makes one kind of mobility the real one. Absolute mobility answers a question about material progress: are people living better than their parents did? Relative mobility answers a question about fairness: does birth still decide where one ends up? Both questions matter, and neither is easy to answer with confidence, since incomes fluctuate and occupations change their meaning across generations. But a society that wants more of the second kind should be honest that it cannot be had at no one's expense, and a society that mourns the loss of the first should not mistake a slower economy for a more rigid one.
